title: UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT
summary: Treat results as sets: combine them, find what they share, and subtract one from another.
intro: Aggregates and `GROUP BY` summarize the rows of one query. Set operators work one level up: two queries with the same columns can be combined like sets. You can stack their rows, keep what they share, or subtract one from the other, all without changing either table.
setup:
CREATE TABLE chess_club (
    name text,
    joined date
);
CREATE TABLE robotics_club (
    name text,
    joined date
);

steps.title: UNION and UNION ALL
steps.body:
This lesson uses two club rosters with the same columns, and three people belong to both:

```sql
CREATE TABLE chess_club (name text, joined date);
CREATE TABLE robotics_club (name text, joined date);
```

| table | members |
| --- | --- |
| chess_club | Ana Lopez, Ben Okafor, Chloe Kim, Dev Patel, Eva Novak, Femi Adeyemi |
| robotics_club | Chloe Kim, Eva Novak, Femi Adeyemi, Gus Moreno, Hana Sato, Ivy Chen |

`UNION` stacks the rows of two queries into one result and removes duplicate rows. `UNION ALL` keeps every row. It skips the duplicate check, so it is faster. Use it whenever duplicates are fine or impossible.

```sql
SELECT name, joined FROM chess_club
UNION ALL
SELECT name, joined FROM robotics_club
ORDER BY joined, name;
```

The rules: both queries return the same number of columns, matching columns have compatible types, and the column names come from the first query. A text literal such as `'chess' AS club` labels where each row came from. One `ORDER BY` at the very end sorts the whole combined result, and it can name only the result's columns, such as `name`, not an expression like `upper(name)`. Mixing types fails. Try this in the editor:

```sql
SELECT name FROM chess_club
UNION
SELECT joined FROM robotics_club;
```

```text
ERROR:  UNION types text and date cannot be matched
```

steps.title: INTERSECT and EXCEPT
steps.body:
The other two set operators compare the rows of two queries instead of stacking them. They follow the same rules as `UNION`: same number of columns, compatible types, one `ORDER BY` at the end.

- `INTERSECT` keeps the rows that appear in both results.
- `EXCEPT` keeps the rows of the first result that are not in the second.

```sql
SELECT name FROM chess_club
INTERSECT
SELECT name FROM robotics_club
ORDER BY name;
```

With `chess_club` and `robotics_club` (each a `name` and a `joined` date), that finds the people in both clubs. Order matters for `EXCEPT`: chess `EXCEPT` robotics is chess-only members, and robotics `EXCEPT` chess is robotics-only members.

Each query can have its own `WHERE` (or even its own `GROUP BY`), which runs before the comparison:

```sql
SELECT name
FROM chess_club
WHERE joined >= DATE '2024-01-01'
EXCEPT
SELECT name FROM robotics_club
ORDER BY name;
```

The gotcha: rows match only when every column matches. `SELECT name, joined` on both sides of `INTERSECT` returns 0 rows here, because each person joined the two clubs on different dates. Unlike `=`, these operators treat two `NULL` values as equal, so a `NULL` on each side matches. Like `UNION`, both operators remove duplicates unless you add `ALL`.

example.title: Shared and chess-only members
example.prompt: Find the members of both clubs, then the chess members who are not in robotics.
example.code:
SELECT name FROM chess_club
INTERSECT
SELECT name FROM robotics_club
ORDER BY name;

SELECT name FROM chess_club
EXCEPT
SELECT name FROM robotics_club
ORDER BY name;
example.output:
name
--------------
 Chloe Kim
 Eva Novak
 Femi Adeyemi
(3 rows)

    name
------------
 Ana Lopez
 Ben Okafor
 Dev Patel
(3 rows)
example.explanation: `INTERSECT` keeps only the names that both queries return. `EXCEPT` starts from every chess name and removes any name the robotics query returns, so Chloe, Eva, and Femi disappear. Only names are compared, so the different join dates do not matter.

practice.title: Robotics only and early overlap
practice.prompt:
Find who does robotics without chess, and which shared members joined chess early.

1. Select the `name` of robotics members who are not in `chess_club`, using `EXCEPT`, sorted by `name`.
2. Select the `name` of chess members who joined before `2024-01-01`, combine it with `INTERSECT` and every `name` in `robotics_club`, and sort by `name`.

Expected output:

```text
    name
------------

 Hana Sato
 Ivy Chen
(3 rows)

   name
-----------

(2 rows)
```

EXCEPT
SELECT name FROM chess_club
ORDER BY name;

recap:
- `UNION` combines two results and removes duplicate rows. `UNION ALL` keeps every row.
- Both queries need the same number of columns with compatible types. Column names come from the first query.
- One `ORDER BY` at the end sorts the whole combined result.
- `INTERSECT` keeps rows found in both results.
- `EXCEPT` keeps rows of the first result that are not in the second, so order matters.
- Rows match only when every column matches, and two `NULL` values count as a match.
